specStatements.text: The stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of the distance the vehicle travels during the driver’s reaction time (thinking distance) and the distance it travels under the braking force (braking distance). For a given braking force the greater the speed of the vehicle, the greater the stopping distance.
(Physics only) Students should be able to estimate how the distance for a vehicle to make an emergency stop varies over a range of speeds typical for that vehicle.
(Physics only) Students will be required to interpret graphs relating speed to stopping distance for a range of vehicles.
Reaction times vary from person to person. Typical values range from 0. 2 s to 0.9 s.
A driver’s reaction time can be affected by tiredness, drugs and alcohol. Distractions may also affect a driver’s ability to react.
Students should be able to:
• explain methods used to measure human reaction times and recall typical results
• interpret and evaluate measurements from simple methods to measure the different reaction times of students
• evaluate the effect of various factors on thinking distance based on given data.
The braking distance of a vehicle can be affected by adverse road and weather conditions and poor condition of the vehicle.
Adverse road conditions include wet or icy conditions. Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.
Students should be able to:
• explain the factors which affect the distance required for road transport vehicles to come to rest in emergencies, and the implications for safety
• estimate how the distance required for road vehicles to stop in an emergency varies over a range of typical speeds.

When a force is applied to the brakes of a vehicle, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.
The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance.
The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle. Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control.
Students should be able to:
• explain the dangers caused by large decelerations
• (HT only) estimate the forces involved in the deceleration of road vehicles in typical situations on a public road.

scopeNotes.statement: Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Everything taught here about the vehicle's own condition refers only to the brakes (for example worn pads) and the tyres (for example little tread depth). Engine, gearbox, suspension and steering are never presented as causes of a longer braking distance; where they appear as distractors (q14) the rationale states explicitly that the specification limits vehicle condition to brakes and tyres.

The two estimating and graph-interpretation statements (S02, S03) are labelled Physics only. This content is written for AQA GCSE Physics (8463), the separate-science specification, so they are in scope and are taught in full. No attempt is made to extend them into Combined Science material.

Estimating the forces involved in the deceleration of road vehicles is Higher Tier only. The one concept (c19), the four misconceptions (m30-m33) and the two questions (q24, q25) built on it are all tiered 'higher'; no Foundation-tier item requires a force to be calculated from a deceleration.

concepts.definition: The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle comes to rest. It is the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time (thinking distance) and the distance travelled under the braking force (braking distance): stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied. The vehicle is still moving at its original speed throughout, so thinking distance = speed x reaction time. It is therefore directly proportional to speed: double the speed and the thinking distance doubles.

The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force, measured from the moment the brakes are applied to the moment the vehicle stops. It depends on the speed, the braking force, the road and weather conditions and the condition of the vehicle's brakes and tyres.

concepts.term: Effect of speed on stopping distance
concepts.definition: For a given braking force the greater the speed of the vehicle, the greater the stopping distance. Both parts grow: the thinking distance grows in proportion to speed, and the braking distance grows more steeply still, because the work the brakes must do equals the kinetic energy of the vehicle, and kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed.

Reaction times vary from person to person. Typical values range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s. That spread matters on the road: at 13 m/s (about 30 mph) a reaction time of 0.2 s gives a thinking distance of about 2.6 m, while 0.9 s gives about 12 m from the same speed.

concepts.term: Factors affecting a driver's reaction time
concepts.definition: A driver's reaction time can be affected by tiredness, drugs and alcohol. Each of these lengthens the reaction time, so at any given speed they lengthen the thinking distance and therefore the stopping distance. They do not change the braking distance.

Distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react - for example using a mobile phone, adjusting the radio or talking to passengers. Like tiredness, drugs and alcohol, a distraction acts on the reaction time and so on the thinking distance, leaving the braking distance unchanged.

concepts.term: Measuring reaction time: the ruler drop method
concepts.definition: One student holds a ruler vertically with the zero mark between the open thumb and finger of a second student, then releases it without warning. The catcher closes their fingers as soon as they see it move. The distance the ruler falls is measured and converted into a time using a conversion chart, because the ruler is in free fall. A shorter fall means a shorter reaction time.

concepts.term: Measuring reaction time: computer methods and typical results
concepts.definition: Reaction time can also be measured with a computer or tablet program in which the user clicks or taps as soon as a shape appears or a sound is played; the machine times the response itself, so the experimenter's own reaction time cannot creep into the result. Typical classroom results are about 0.2 s to 0.3 s, at the fast end of the 0.2 s to 0.9 s range.

Repeat the test several times for each student, identify any clearly anomalous result and leave it out, then calculate a mean of the rest. Keep everything else the same - the same ruler, the same starting gap between the fingers, no countdown before the drop - so that any difference between students is due to reaction time and not to the way the test was run.

concepts.term: Judging the effect of a factor on thinking distance from data
concepts.definition: To evaluate how a factor such as tiredness, alcohol or a phone call affects thinking distance, compare thinking distances measured at the same speed. Dividing a thinking distance by the speed converts it back to a reaction time, which allows results taken at different speeds to be compared fairly.

The braking distance of a vehicle can be affected by adverse road and weather conditions. Adverse road conditions include wet or icy conditions. They reduce the grip between the tyres and the road, so the vehicle travels further before it stops. They have no effect on the driver's reaction time, so the thinking distance is unchanged.

Braking distance is also increased by poor condition of the vehicle. Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres - for example worn brake pads that cannot produce the full braking force, or tyres with too little tread to clear water from the road surface.

concepts.term: Estimating stopping distance at typical speeds
concepts.definition: Estimate the thinking distance from thinking distance = speed x reaction time, using a reaction time of about 0.7 s for an alert driver. Estimate the braking distance from the braking deceleration using v2 - u2 = 2 a s, which is given in the exam; a typical family car on a dry road decelerates at about 6.5 m/s2. At 13 m/s (about 30 mph) that gives roughly 9 m + 13 m = 22 m, and at 27 m/s (about 60 mph) roughly 19 m + 56 m = 75 m.

Plotted against speed, thinking distance is a straight line through the origin, while braking distance is a curve that rises ever more steeply. The total stopping distance curve therefore also becomes steeper as speed increases. When two vehicles are plotted together, the one whose line lies higher needs the greater distance to stop at every speed.

concepts.term: Work done by the braking friction force
concepts.definition: When a force is applied to the brakes of a vehicle, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases. Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the vehicle to the thermal store of the brakes; none of it is destroyed.

The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance. The work done by the brakes is the braking force multiplied by the braking distance, and it must equal the kinetic energy of the vehicle; so if the distance is fixed, a vehicle with more kinetic energy needs a larger force.

concepts.term: Braking force, deceleration and its dangers
concepts.definition: The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle. Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control. Overheated brakes become less effective, and a vehicle that skids can no longer be steered.

concepts.term: Estimating the force in a deceleration
concepts.definition: (HT only) Estimate the deceleration first, either from acceleration = change in velocity / time taken, or from v2 - u2 = 2 a s, which is given in the exam. Then use resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a, which must be recalled. A typical family car has a mass of about 1000 kg to 1500 kg, so an emergency stop at about 6.5 m/s2 needs a braking force of roughly 7000 N to 10 000 N.

Because stopping distance rises with speed, and rises further in wet or icy conditions or with worn brakes or tyres, safe driving means leaving a gap big enough to cover the whole stopping distance and cutting speed when conditions are poor. Speed limits, minimum tyre tread depths and brake testing all exist because those factors change how far a vehicle needs in order to stop.

misconceptions.question: A car's speed doubles. What happens to the thinking distance, if the driver's reaction time is unchanged?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles, because thinking distance = speed x reaction time and the reaction time has not changed.
misconceptions.misconception: Thinking distance is about how fast you think, so it is the same however fast you are going.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'thinking distance' invites students to treat it as a property of the driver. Reaction time genuinely is a property of the driver and does not change with speed, and students then attach that fixed-ness to the distance as well.
misconceptions.correction: The reaction time is fixed, but the car keeps moving at its full speed throughout that time. Distance = speed x time, so at twice the speed the car covers twice as much road in the same reaction time.

misconceptions.question: A car's speed doubles from 15 m/s to 30 m/s. What happens to the braking distance for the same braking force?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes about four times as large, because the work the brakes must do equals the kinetic energy, which depends on speed squared.
misconceptions.misconception: If you go twice as fast you need twice the distance to brake - everything just doubles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Thinking distance really does double, so students apply the same proportional rule to the braking distance without checking it against data or against the energy argument.
misconceptions.correction: Braking force x braking distance = kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed squared. With the force fixed, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy and so quadruples the braking distance. Typical data show this: at 30 mph the braking distance is about 14 m, at 60 mph about 55 m.

misconceptions.question: What does the stopping distance of a vehicle include?
misconceptions.correct: Both the thinking distance and the braking distance - the whole distance from seeing the hazard to coming to rest.
misconceptions.misconception: Stopping distance means the distance it takes to stop once you have hit the brakes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'stopping' begins when the brakes go on. The thinking phase feels like nothing is happening, even though the car is covering ground at full speed.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force. At 30 mph the thinking part is about 9 m of the 23 m total - well over a third.

misconceptions.question: Does the braking distance of a car depend on anything other than how hard the brakes are applied?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. For a given braking force the braking distance still depends on the speed, and also on the road conditions and the state of the brakes and tyres.
misconceptions.misconception: The braking distance is set by the brakes, so as long as you brake just as hard you will stop in the same distance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that a bigger braking force gives a shorter stop, then treat the braking force as the only variable and forget that it has to remove a quantity of kinetic energy that depends on speed.
misconceptions.correction: The brakes must do work equal to the vehicle's kinetic energy. With the force fixed, a faster vehicle has more kinetic energy to remove, so the brakes must act over a longer distance.

misconceptions.question: Are the thinking distance and the braking distance always about the same size?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are similar only at low speed; as speed rises the braking distance becomes much the larger of the two.
misconceptions.misconception: Thinking distance and braking distance are roughly equal, so the stopping distance is just double the thinking distance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In the familiar Highway Code table the 20 mph row shows 6 m and 6 m, and that first row is the one students remember. It is the only row in which the two are equal.
misconceptions.correction: Thinking distance grows in proportion to speed while braking distance grows with speed squared, so they separate quickly. At 70 mph the figures are about 21 m thinking and 75 m braking.

misconceptions.question: On a graph of stopping distance against speed, two vehicles are plotted. What does the higher line mean?
misconceptions.correct: The vehicle on the higher line needs a greater distance to stop from any given speed.
misconceptions.misconception: The line that is higher up the graph must be the better vehicle - it is ahead of the other one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over an everyday reading of graphs in which 'higher is better', as with test scores or performance charts, instead of reading the y-axis label.
misconceptions.correction: Read the axis. The y-axis is a distance needed in order to stop, so a higher line means a longer, and therefore worse, stopping distance at that speed.

misconceptions.question: A car has badly worn tyres and is carrying a heavy load. Does that lengthen the thinking distance?
misconceptions.correct: No. Thinking distance depends only on the driver's reaction time and the speed of the vehicle.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that makes a car harder to stop must make the thinking distance longer as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn a list of factors that increase stopping distance and do not sort it into the two separate parts, so every factor gets attached to both.
misconceptions.correction: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time. Worn tyres and heavy loads cannot change either of those, so they act on the braking distance only. Sort every factor into 'driver' (thinking) or 'road and vehicle' (braking).

misconceptions.question: What is a typical human reaction time?
misconceptions.correct: Reaction times vary from person to person, with typical values ranging from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
misconceptions.misconception: Everyone's reaction time is about the same - roughly one second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One second is the round number students reach for, and the Highway Code figures happen to be based on a reaction time of about 0.7 s, which rounds up to 'about a second' in most retellings.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the specification's range: 0.2 s to 0.9 s, and expect real variation between people. Even within the range, the slowest driver's thinking distance is over four times the fastest driver's at the same speed.

misconceptions.question: Could a driver have a reaction time of 0.02 s?
misconceptions.correct: No. Typical human reaction times range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s, ten to forty times longer than that.
misconceptions.misconception: Reacting feels instant, so the reaction time must be a tiny fraction of a second - a few hundredths.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The experience of reacting carries no sense of duration, and students confuse the speed of a nerve impulse with the whole see-decide-move sequence.
misconceptions.correction: The signal has to travel to the brain, be processed, and travel back to the muscles, which move a limb. Measured values in the ruler drop test are around 0.2 s, matching the bottom of the specification's range.

misconceptions.question: An icy road lengthens the stopping distance. Which part of it does the ice lengthen?
misconceptions.correct: The braking distance only. Road and weather conditions do not change the driver's reaction time.
misconceptions.misconception: Ice and rain make everything worse, so the thinking distance goes up too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know bad weather makes driving more dangerous overall, and attach that general danger to both parts of the stopping distance rather than asking which mechanism is affected.
misconceptions.correction: Ice reduces the grip between tyres and road, which affects how far the car travels once the brakes are on. The reaction time is a property of the driver, so the thinking distance at a given speed is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: In the ruler drop test the ruler falls 20 cm before it is caught. Is the reaction time 20?
misconceptions.correct: No. The 20 cm must be converted into a time; a 20 cm fall corresponds to a reaction time of about 0.2 s.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of centimetres the ruler falls is the reaction time - you just read it off the ruler.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Some printed rulers used for the test have a time scale marked alongside the centimetre scale, so students remember reading a value off the ruler without noticing which scale it came from.
misconceptions.correction: The ruler measures a distance in centimetres, not a time in seconds. The ruler falls freely under gravity, so the fall distance is converted to a time using a chart or the free-fall relationship.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter whether the catcher is counted down before the ruler is released?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The ruler must be released without warning, or the catcher can anticipate the drop and the result is not a reaction time.
misconceptions.misconception: Saying 'three, two, one, go' just makes the test fairer, since everyone gets the same warning.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate fair testing with treating everyone identically, and a countdown feels like the fairest possible start signal.
misconceptions.correction: The test measures the time to react to seeing the ruler move. A countdown lets the catcher predict the moment and close their fingers on the count instead, giving an impossibly short 'reaction time'. Keeping everything else the same is what makes the test fair.

misconceptions.question: A student's five ruler drop results are 0.19 s, 0.21 s, 0.20 s, 0.55 s and 0.20 s. Which value should be quoted?
misconceptions.correct: The mean of the four consistent results, about 0.20 s, with the 0.55 s treated as anomalous.
misconceptions.misconception: Quote the quickest result - that is what you can really do when you concentrate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reaction time feels like a personal best, and in sport the best performance is the one that counts. Students transfer that habit into the laboratory.
misconceptions.correction: A single quickest value may be a lucky anticipation rather than a genuine reaction. A mean of repeated readings, with clear anomalies excluded, is the more reliable estimate.

misconceptions.question: Four results cluster near 0.20 s and one is 0.55 s. Should the 0.55 s go into the mean?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is anomalous - far outside the spread of the others - so it should be identified and left out of the mean.
misconceptions.misconception: You have to include every measurement you made; throwing one away is fixing the data.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are rightly taught not to discard inconvenient results, and cannot yet tell the difference between discarding data that disagrees with a prediction and excluding a reading that is clearly the product of a mistake.
misconceptions.correction: Anomalies are excluded because something went wrong in that trial - a fumble, a distraction - not because the value is inconvenient. State that the result was anomalous and why, then take the mean of the rest.

misconceptions.question: At 13 m/s a driver's thinking distance rises from 9 m to 15 m after drinking alcohol. By how much has the reaction time risen?
misconceptions.correct: By about 0.5 s: 9/13 = 0.69 s and 15/13 = 1.15 s, a difference of about 0.46 s.
misconceptions.misconception: The thinking distance went up by 6, so the reaction time went up by 6 seconds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students subtract the two given numbers and carry the answer straight across to whatever quantity the question asks about, without checking units.
misconceptions.correction: Metres are not seconds. Divide each thinking distance by the speed to get a reaction time, then subtract. A 6 m increase at 13 m/s corresponds to an extra 0.46 s.

misconceptions.question: A driver has been drinking alcohol. Which part of the stopping distance is increased?
misconceptions.correct: The thinking distance. Alcohol lengthens the driver's reaction time; the braking distance is unaffected.
misconceptions.misconception: Alcohol and drugs make the whole car harder to stop, so the braking distance goes up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Road safety campaigns say drink-driving means 'you cannot stop in time', and students turn that general warning into a statement about the brakes.
misconceptions.correction: Alcohol and drugs act on the driver, not on the vehicle. They lengthen the reaction time and therefore the thinking distance. Braking distance is changed by the road, the weather and the vehicle's brakes and tyres.

misconceptions.question: A driver is tired at the end of a long journey. Does this lengthen the braking distance?
misconceptions.correct: No. Tiredness lengthens the reaction time and so the thinking distance; the braking distance is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: A tired driver cannot brake properly, so the braking distance must be longer as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture a tired driver braking feebly and slowly, mixing the driver's alertness up with the force the brakes can generate.
misconceptions.correction: Braking distance is decided by the braking force, the speed, the road conditions and the state of brakes and tyres. Tiredness is one of the factors the specification lists as affecting reaction time, alongside drugs and alcohol.

misconceptions.question: A car has a worn engine and a noisy gearbox. Does this increase the braking distance?
misconceptions.correct: No. For this specification, poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.
misconceptions.misconception: Any part of a car that is worn out will make it take longer to stop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Poor condition of the vehicle' sounds like a description of the whole car, so students list every component they can think of rather than the two the specification names.
misconceptions.correction: The specification limits poor vehicle condition to the brakes or the tyres. Worn pads reduce the braking force; worn tyres reduce grip. The engine and gearbox drive the car forward and play no part in stopping it.

misconceptions.question: Do worn tyres affect a vehicle's braking distance?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Tyres are named alongside brakes as the parts whose poor condition lengthens the braking distance.
misconceptions.misconception: Tyres are about grip and cornering; it is the brakes that stop the car, so only the brakes matter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'brakes' is in 'braking distance', which makes the brakes look like the only relevant component, and the role of the tyres in transmitting that braking to the road is invisible.
misconceptions.correction: Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres - both count. Tyres with too little tread cannot clear water or hold the road, so the vehicle travels further before stopping.

misconceptions.question: Why is the braking distance longer on an icy road?
misconceptions.correct: Because the ice reduces the grip between the tyres and the road, so the vehicle travels further before it comes to rest.
misconceptions.misconception: The ice gets into the brakes so the brakes cannot grip the wheel any more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the friction force in braking acts between the brakes and the wheel, and reasonably assume that any slippery condition must be attacking that same surface.
misconceptions.correction: Braking involves two separate frictional contacts: the brakes on the wheel, and the tyres on the road. Ice and water affect the tyre-road contact, so the wheels can lock or slip while the brakes themselves work normally.

misconceptions.question: A car brakes to rest. What happens to its kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: Work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel transfers it to the thermal store of the brakes, whose temperature increases.
misconceptions.misconception: The kinetic energy is destroyed by the friction in the brakes - once the car stops, it has gone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Friction is introduced as the force that 'takes energy away', and because the car ends up motionless the energy appears to have vanished with the motion.
misconceptions.correction: Energy cannot be destroyed, only transferred. The work done against friction raises the temperature of the brakes, and that thermal energy is then dissipated to the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: Do the brakes store the car's kinetic energy and give it back when the car sets off again?
misconceptions.correct: No. The energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes, raising their temperature, and is then dissipated to the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: The brakes hold on to the energy, like a stretched spring, and release it again when you accelerate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet elastic potential energy first, where storing and returning energy is exactly what happens, and generalise that reversible picture to every energy transfer.
misconceptions.correction: Friction transfers energy to thermal stores and spreads it out; that transfer is not reversible. Energy to accelerate the car again comes from its fuel or battery, not from the hot brakes.

misconceptions.question: Why do a lorry's brakes get hot on a long descent?
misconceptions.correct: Because work is done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel, transferring energy to the thermal store of the brakes.
misconceptions.misconception: The heat comes from the engine - the engine is working hard, and heat spreads to the brakes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The engine is the obvious hot part of a vehicle in everyday experience, so any heating is attributed to it rather than to the work done against friction at the brakes.
misconceptions.correction: The temperature rise is produced at the brakes themselves by the work done against friction, and it is largest when the brakes have removed the most kinetic energy - which is why long descents and repeated hard stops overheat them.

misconceptions.question: As a braking car loses kinetic energy, what happens to the temperature of its brakes?
misconceptions.correct: It increases, because work done against friction transfers energy into the thermal store of the brakes.
misconceptions.misconception: The car is losing energy, so everything about it is cooling down, including the brakes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Losing energy' is read as 'having less of everything', and students do not track where the energy goes as it is transferred out of the kinetic store.
misconceptions.correction: The vehicle loses kinetic energy, but that energy arrives somewhere: in the brakes. The specification is explicit that the temperature of the brakes increases.

misconceptions.question: Two identical cars must stop in the same distance, one from 15 m/s and one from 30 m/s. Do they need the same braking force?
misconceptions.correct: No. The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop it in a certain distance.
misconceptions.misconception: The brakes on a car always produce the same force; going faster just means they have to act for longer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A brake feels like a fixed component with one setting, and students who have grasped that the same brakes are fitted to both cars conclude the force must therefore be the same.
misconceptions.correction: The braking force depends on how hard the brakes are applied, and it is set by what the stop demands: force x braking distance must equal the kinetic energy. Over the same distance, the faster car needs the larger force.

misconceptions.question: A driver presses the brake pedal harder. What happens to the deceleration?
misconceptions.correct: It increases. The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle.
misconceptions.misconception: Deceleration is a negative acceleration, so a bigger braking force makes the acceleration smaller - which means a smaller deceleration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The minus sign is doing real work here: -8 m/s2 is a smaller number than -4 m/s2, and students who reason with the signed value conclude the deceleration has been reduced.
misconceptions.correction: Deceleration is the size of the negative acceleration. A larger braking force gives a more negative acceleration, which is a larger deceleration - the vehicle slows more sharply.

misconceptions.question: What dangers can a very large deceleration lead to?
misconceptions.correct: Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control.
misconceptions.misconception: Braking hard cools the brakes down suddenly, and the danger is that they seize up when they get cold.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who remember only that braking changes the temperature of the brakes have a fifty-fifty chance of remembering the direction wrongly, and 'cooling' fits the idea of the car losing energy.
misconceptions.correction: Braking raises the temperature of the brakes. A large deceleration transfers energy quickly, so the brakes can overheat and become less effective, and the vehicle may skid and become impossible to steer.

misconceptions.question: What is the kinetic energy of a 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s?
misconceptions.correct: 240 000 J, from kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed squared = 0.5 x 1200 x 20 x 20.
misconceptions.misconception: Kinetic energy is 0.5 x mass x speed, so it is 0.5 x 1200 x 20 = 12 000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is usually written as 0.5 m v2, and in a rushed calculation the small superscript 2 is the easiest part of it to lose.
misconceptions.correction: The speed is squared. Write the substitution out in full - 0.5 x 1200 x 20 x 20 - so the square cannot be dropped. It is the squaring that makes braking distance grow so steeply with speed.

misconceptions.question: A car's kinetic energy is 240 000 J and it stops in 40 m. What braking force was needed?
misconceptions.correct: 6000 N. Work done = force x distance, so force = 240 000 / 40 = 6000 N.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy is 240 000, so the force is 240 000 N - it is the same number, just written differently.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy and force are both 'how strong the effect is' in everyday language, and once a big number has been calculated students are reluctant to believe another step is needed.
misconceptions.correction: Joules and newtons are different quantities. Work done = force x distance, so the energy must be divided by the distance over which the force acts to give the force in newtons.

misconceptions.question: A car slows from 20 m/s to rest in 25 m. What is its deceleration?
misconceptions.correct: 8 m/s2, from v2 - u2 = 2 a s: 0 - 400 = 2 x a x 25, so a = -8 m/s2.
misconceptions.misconception: You can just do 400 divided by 25, because the 2 in the equation does not really change anything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 2 sits between two symbols in a formula the student is copying rather than reading, and dropping it produces an answer that still looks reasonable.
misconceptions.correction: Substitute into v2 - u2 = 2 a s exactly as it is given on the equation sheet. The factor of 2 halves the acceleration, and here it is the difference between 16 m/s2 and 8 m/s2.

misconceptions.question: A car slows from 20 m/s to rest over 25 m. Is the deceleration 20/25 = 0.8 m/s2?
misconceptions.correct: No. Acceleration is a change in velocity divided by a time, or found from v2 - u2 = 2 a s; here it is 8 m/s2.
misconceptions.misconception: Acceleration is speed divided by distance, so dividing 20 by 25 gives it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that acceleration is 'speed divided by something' and reach for whichever other number the question supplies - here a distance rather than a time.
misconceptions.correction: Check the units. Velocity divided by distance gives 1/s, not m/s2. Use acceleration = change in velocity / time taken when a time is given, and v2 - u2 = 2 a s when a distance is given.

misconceptions.question: A 1200 kg car is travelling at 13 m/s. Is the braking force 1200 x 13 = 15 600 N?
misconceptions.correct: No. That product is the momentum, in kg m/s. Force = mass x acceleration, so the deceleration must be found first.
misconceptions.misconception: Force is mass times velocity - you multiply the two numbers the question gives you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: F = m a and p = m v look almost identical, and the velocity is the quantity actually printed in the question while the acceleration has to be worked out.
misconceptions.correction: Find the deceleration first, from a = change in velocity / time or from v2 - u2 = 2 a s, then substitute into resultant force = mass x acceleration.

misconceptions.question: A 1200 kg car stops in 4.0 s. Is the braking force 1200 x 4.0 = 4800 N?
misconceptions.correct: No. F = m a needs the acceleration, not the time. Here a = 13/4.0 = 3.25 m/s2, so the force is about 3900 N.
misconceptions.misconception: In F = m a you can put the time in for a if you have not worked the acceleration out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acceleration and time are both about how the motion changes over the stop, and under exam pressure students substitute the number they already have rather than doing the extra step.
misconceptions.correction: Work out the acceleration first: change in velocity divided by time taken. Only then substitute into F = m a. Checking units catches this - kg x s is not a newton.

misconceptions.question: Is the kinetic energy of a 1200 kg car at 20 m/s equal to 1200 x 20 x 20 = 480 000 J?
misconceptions.correct: No. Kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed squared, so it is 240 000 J.
misconceptions.misconception: You square the speed and multiply by the mass; the 0.5 is a detail you can leave out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The squared term feels like the important part of the equation, and a factor of one half looks decorative next to it.
misconceptions.correction: The 0.5 is part of the equation and halves the answer. Every braking force calculated from kinetic energy will be twice too large without it.

mcqs.stem: A driver sees a hazard ahead and brings the car safely to rest. What is the stopping distance of the car?

options.text: The thinking distance added to the braking distance.
options.rationale: The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force.

options.text: The distance travelled once the brakes are applied.
options.rationale: That is the braking distance alone. Students take 'stopping' to begin at the moment the brake pedal is pressed, ignoring the ground covered while the driver reacts.

options.text: Twice the thinking distance, as the two parts match.
options.rationale: The 20 mph row of the familiar data table has equal thinking and braking distances, and students generalise that coincidence to every speed.

options.text: The distance travelled during the reaction time.
options.rationale: That is the thinking distance alone. It leaves out the braking distance, which is the larger part at anything above low speed.

mcqs.stem: A car is driven faster along the same road, and the braking force the brakes can produce is unchanged. What happens to the stopping distance?

options.text: Only the braking distance grows; thinking distance is fixed.
options.rationale: The student treats thinking distance as a property of the driver, forgetting that the car keeps moving at its full speed during the reaction time.

options.text: It rises: both the thinking and braking distances grow.
options.rationale: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time, so it grows with speed, and a faster car has more kinetic energy for the same braking force to remove, so the braking distance grows too.

options.text: Only the thinking distance grows; braking distance is fixed.
options.rationale: The student assumes that the braking distance is set purely by how hard the brakes are applied, so an unchanged braking force must mean an unchanged distance.

options.text: It stays the same, because the braking force is unchanged.
options.rationale: The student latches onto the one quantity the question says is constant and concludes that the outcome must be constant as well.

mcqs.stem: A driver with a reaction time of 0.70 s is driving at 20 m/s when a hazard appears. What is the thinking distance?

options.rationale: The student works out 14 m and then doubles it, believing the braking distance always matches the thinking distance - and answers with the stopping distance instead.
The student ignores the 0.70 s given and uses a reaction time of about 1 s, the value they assume applies to everyone.
Thinking distance = speed x reaction time = 20 m/s x 0.70 s = 14 m.
The student divides 0.70 by 20 instead of multiplying, a common slip when it is unclear which way round the quantities go.

mcqs.stem: A car's speed doubles from 15 m/s to 30 m/s. The driver's reaction time and the braking force are unchanged. What happens to the two parts of the stopping distance?

options.text: Thinking distance doubles and the braking distance is unchanged.
options.rationale: The student treats the braking distance as fixed by the brakes alone, since the question says the braking force has not changed.

options.text: Thinking distance is unchanged and the braking distance doubles.
options.rationale: The student holds the thinking distance fixed because the reaction time is fixed, and applies the doubling only to the part that involves the brakes.

options.text: Both the thinking distance and the braking distance simply double.
options.rationale: Doubling really does apply to the thinking distance, and the student extends the same proportional rule to the braking distance without testing it.

options.text: Thinking distance doubles; braking distance rises about four times.
options.rationale: Thinking distance is proportional to speed. The brakes must do work equal to the kinetic energy, which is proportional to speed squared, so with the force fixed the braking distance quadruples.

mcqs.stem: Stopping distance is plotted on the vertical axis against speed on the horizontal axis for one car. What shape is the graph?

options.text: A curve that gets steeper, as braking distance grows fastest.
options.rationale: Thinking distance contributes a straight line, but braking distance grows with speed squared, so the total curves upwards and its gradient increases with speed.

options.text: A straight line from the origin, as distance follows speed.
options.rationale: The student assumes both parts are proportional to speed, which is true of the thinking distance only, and so predicts a straight line.

options.text: A horizontal line, because the braking force does not change.
options.rationale: The student reasons that if the brakes are unchanged then the distance needed to stop must be unchanged too, whatever the speed.

options.text: A curve that flattens off, as the brakes work harder at speed.
options.rationale: The student assumes the braking system somehow compensates at high speed, so each extra unit of speed costs less extra distance.

mcqs.stem: Stopping distance against speed is plotted for a car and for a loaded lorry on the same axes. The lorry's line lies above the car's line at every speed. What does this show?

options.text: At any given speed the lorry comes to rest more quickly.
options.rationale: The student reads the graph with the everyday rule that a higher line means better performance, without checking what the vertical axis measures.

options.text: At any given speed the lorry needs a longer distance to stop.
options.rationale: The vertical axis is the distance needed in order to stop, so the higher line is the vehicle that needs more distance from the same speed.

options.text: The lorry's heavy load makes its driver's reaction time longer.
options.rationale: The student attaches a vehicle property to the thinking distance, which in fact depends only on the driver's reaction time and the speed.

options.text: The lorry is always driven faster than the car on that road.
options.rationale: The student confuses the vertical separation of the lines with a difference in speed, although speed is the horizontal axis and is the same for both.

mcqs.stem: Which range gives the typical values of human reaction time?

options.text: 1.0 s to 3.0 s
options.rationale: The student pictures the whole see-decide-brake sequence as taking a couple of seconds, well beyond the measured range.

options.text: 0.5 s to 1.5 s
options.rationale: The student centres the range on 'about one second', the round figure usually quoted for a driver.

options.text: 0.2 s to 0.9 s
options.rationale: These are the typical values given in the specification, and they match measured classroom results of about 0.2 s.
Reacting feels instantaneous, so the student assumes a time of hundredths of a second.

mcqs.stem: Which of these would increase a driver's thinking distance at a given speed?

options.text: The road ahead is covered with ice and slush.
options.rationale: Ice increases the braking distance by reducing grip, but it cannot change the driver's reaction time. The student applies bad conditions to both parts.

options.text: The tyres are worn below the legal tread depth.
options.rationale: Worn tyres lengthen the braking distance. The student attaches a vehicle fault to the thinking distance as well.

options.text: The car is loaded with heavy luggage and cases.
options.rationale: A heavy load acts on the vehicle, not on the driver's reaction, so it cannot change the thinking distance.

options.text: The driver is tired at the end of a long shift.
options.rationale: Tiredness is one of the factors the specification names as affecting reaction time, and thinking distance = speed x reaction time.

mcqs.stem: A ruler drop test is used to measure a student's reaction time. Which statement about the method is correct?

options.text: The distance the ruler falls is measured and converted to a time.
options.rationale: The ruler falls freely under gravity, so the measured fall distance is converted into a reaction time using a chart or the free-fall relationship.

options.text: The number of centimetres the ruler falls is the reaction time.
options.rationale: The student reads a value off the ruler and quotes it as a time, because some test rulers carry a time scale alongside the centimetre scale.

options.text: The catcher is told exactly when the ruler will be released.
options.rationale: A countdown feels like the fairest way to start, but it lets the catcher anticipate the drop rather than react to it.

options.text: A stopwatch times the fall, avoiding any human reaction error.
options.rationale: Timing such a short fall by hand adds the experimenter's own reaction time twice over, which is exactly the error the ruler method avoids.

mcqs.stem: A class measures reaction times using the ruler drop test. Which result is typical for a student?

options.text: About 2.00 s
options.rationale: The student misplaces the decimal point, or imagines the whole see-and-catch action taking a couple of seconds.

options.text: About 0.20 s
options.rationale: A typical fall of around 20 cm corresponds to about 0.2 s, at the fast end of the 0.2 s to 0.9 s range.

options.text: About 1.20 s
options.rationale: The student assumes everyone's reaction time is around a second, above the specification's stated range.

options.text: About 0.02 s
options.rationale: Catching feels instant, so the student picks a value ten times shorter than any measured human reaction.

mcqs.stem: One student's five ruler drop results are 0.19 s, 0.21 s, 0.20 s, 0.55 s and 0.20 s. How should these results be treated?

options.text: Take the smallest value, as that is the true reaction time.
options.rationale: The student treats the test like a sporting personal best, where the quickest attempt is the one that counts.

options.text: Take the mean of all five, as no result can be left out.
options.rationale: The student has learned never to discard data and cannot yet distinguish an anomaly from an inconvenient value.

options.text: Treat 0.55 s as anomalous; take the mean of the other four.
options.rationale: 0.55 s lies far outside the tight spread of the other readings, so it is identified as anomalous and excluded, and the mean of the remaining four is quoted.

options.text: Take the range of the values and quote that as the result.
options.rationale: The range describes the spread of the data; it is not an estimate of the quantity being measured.

mcqs.stem: Data for one driver at 13 m/s show a thinking distance of 9 m when alert and 15 m after drinking alcohol. What do these data show?

options.text: The alcohol has raised the reaction time by about 6.0 s.
options.rationale: The student subtracts 9 m from 15 m and quotes the difference as a time, carrying a distance across into seconds.

options.text: The alcohol has raised the braking distance by about 6 m.
options.rationale: The student assumes alcohol makes the car harder to stop, and relabels the extra thinking distance as braking distance.

options.text: The alcohol has raised the reaction time by about 1.7 s.
options.rationale: The student divides 15 by 9 to get a ratio of 1.7 and quotes it as an increase in seconds.

options.text: The alcohol has raised the reaction time by about 0.5 s.
options.rationale: 9/13 = 0.69 s and 15/13 = 1.15 s, so the reaction time has risen by about 0.46 s, which rounds to 0.5 s.

mcqs.stem: Which of these increases the braking distance of a car?

options.text: Rain has made the road surface wet and slippery.
options.rationale: Wet conditions are named in the specification as adverse road conditions; less grip between tyres and road means the car travels further under the braking force.

options.text: The driver is tired at the end of a long trip.
options.rationale: Tiredness lengthens the reaction time and so the thinking distance, but it does not change how the brakes act on the car.

options.text: The driver has taken a drug causing drowsiness.
options.rationale: Drugs act on the driver, lengthening the thinking distance; the student assumes they make the whole car harder to stop.

options.text: A radio is playing loudly inside the moving car.
options.rationale: A distraction can lengthen the reaction time and so the thinking distance, but it has no effect on the braking distance.

mcqs.stem: Poor condition of a vehicle can increase its braking distance. Which pair of parts does this cover?

options.text: The brakes and the engine.
options.rationale: The engine drives the car forward and plays no part in stopping it; the student assumes any worn component lengthens the stop.

options.text: The brakes and the tyres.
options.rationale: The specification limits poor condition of the vehicle to the vehicle's brakes or tyres: worn pads reduce the braking force and worn tyres reduce grip.

options.text: The brakes but not the tyres.
options.rationale: The word 'braking' points the student at the brakes alone, hiding the role of the tyres in gripping the road.

options.text: The engine and the gearbox.
options.rationale: Both belong to the system that makes the car go, not the system that stops it, so neither affects braking distance.

mcqs.stem: On an icy road, drivers are advised to leave a much bigger gap to the vehicle in front. Which statement best explains this advice?

options.text: The ice lengthens the driver's reaction time and thinking distance.
options.rationale: The student applies bad conditions to both parts of the stopping distance; the reaction time belongs to the driver and is unaffected by the road.

options.text: The ice stops the brakes from being able to grip the wheel.
options.rationale: The student places the ice at the brake-wheel contact rather than at the tyre-road contact, where it actually acts.

options.text: The ice lengthens the braking distance, so more space is needed.
options.rationale: Ice is an adverse road condition that reduces grip between the tyres and the road, so the vehicle travels further under the braking force and the whole stopping distance grows.

options.text: The ice makes the vehicle travel faster than the speedometer shows.
options.rationale: The student invents a change in speed to explain the longer stop, rather than a change in the distance needed to remove the kinetic energy.

mcqs.stem: A car is travelling at 27 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.70 s and the car decelerates at 6.5 m/s2 while braking. Estimate the stopping distance.

options.rationale: This is the braking distance alone; the student forgets the 19 m covered during the reaction time.
The student works out the 19 m thinking distance and doubles it, assuming the braking distance always matches.
This is the thinking distance alone; the student stops the calculation once the brakes are applied.
Thinking distance = 27 x 0.70 = 19 m. Braking distance from v2 - u2 = 2 a s is 27 x 27 / (2 x 6.5) = 56 m. The total is about 75 m.

mcqs.stem: A car is slowed by applying its brakes. Which description of the energy transfer is correct?

options.text: Work done by friction cuts the kinetic energy and heats the brakes.
options.rationale: Work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.

options.text: Friction in the brakes destroys the kinetic energy of the car.
options.rationale: The car ends up motionless, so the energy appears to the student to have gone rather than been transferred.

options.text: The brakes store the kinetic energy and return it later on.
options.rationale: The student generalises from a stretched spring, where energy really is stored and released, to a frictional transfer that is not reversible.

options.text: The kinetic energy is transferred to the road by the hot tyres.
options.rationale: The student places the heating at the tyre-road contact instead of at the friction between the brakes and the wheel.

mcqs.stem: A lorry brakes hard several times while descending a long hill. What happens to the temperature of its brakes?

options.text: It falls, because the lorry is losing its kinetic energy.
options.rationale: The student reads 'losing energy' as everything cooling, without tracking where the energy is transferred to.

options.text: It rises, because work is done against friction at the brakes.
options.rationale: Each stop transfers kinetic energy into the thermal store of the brakes through the work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel.

options.text: It rises, but only because the engine is working hard.
options.rationale: The engine is the part of a vehicle students associate with heat, so the temperature rise is attributed to it rather than to friction.

options.text: It stays constant while the lorry is still moving.
options.rationale: The student assumes heating only begins once the vehicle has stopped, rather than during the transfer itself.

mcqs.stem: Two identical cars must each be brought to rest in a braking distance of 30 m. One is travelling at 15 m/s, the other at 30 m/s. What can be said about the braking forces needed?

options.text: Both need the same force; only the distance differs.
options.rationale: The student treats braking force as a fixed property of the brakes and looks for the difference somewhere else.

options.text: The faster car needs a smaller, longer-lasting force.
options.rationale: The student pictures a long gentle stop for the faster car, confusing the size of the force with the time for which it acts.

options.text: The faster car needs the greater braking force.
options.rationale: Force x braking distance must equal the kinetic energy removed. Over the same 30 m, the car with more kinetic energy needs the larger force.

options.text: Both cars need exactly the same braking force.
options.rationale: Identical cars have identical brakes, so the student concludes the force must be identical too, ignoring the speed.

mcqs.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 20 m/s and must stop in a braking distance of 40 m. The work done by the brakes equals the car's kinetic energy. What average braking force is needed?

options.rationale: The student leaves the factor of 0.5 out of the kinetic energy, getting 480 000 J and hence twice the correct force.
The student calculates the kinetic energy correctly and then quotes that number as the force, without dividing by the distance.
The student forgets to square the speed, getting 12 000 J for the kinetic energy and dividing that by 40 m.
Kinetic energy = 0.5 x 1200 x 20 x 20 = 240 000 J. Work done = force x distance, so force = 240 000 / 40 = 6000 N.

mcqs.stem: A driver presses the brake pedal harder, which increases the braking force on the car. What happens to the car's motion?

options.text: Its deceleration rises, so it slows down more sharply.
options.rationale: The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle, as resultant force = mass x acceleration.

options.text: Its deceleration falls, so it slows down more gently.
options.rationale: Working with the signed value, the student sees the acceleration becoming a smaller number and reads that as a smaller deceleration.

options.text: Its deceleration is unchanged; the brakes just act longer.
options.rationale: The student treats the brakes as a component with one fixed setting, so a harder press changes only the duration.

options.text: Its deceleration is unchanged; only the distance falls.
options.rationale: The student links the harder braking to the outcome they care about, the shorter stop, without connecting force to deceleration.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of effects are the dangers that a very large deceleration may lead to?

options.text: The brakes may cool too fast and then seize up.
options.rationale: The student remembers that braking changes the temperature of the brakes but recalls the direction of that change wrongly.

options.text: The brakes may overheat and control may be lost.
options.rationale: These are exactly the two dangers the specification names: large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control.

options.text: The engine may overheat and the car may stall.
options.rationale: The student attributes the heating to the engine, the part of a vehicle they associate with getting hot.

options.text: The brakes may wear out and need replacing.
options.rationale: Hard braking does wear brakes, but that is a maintenance cost over time, not the immediate danger the specification identifies.

mcqs.stem: A lorry driver brakes hard again and again while descending a long, steep hill. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: The engine overheats because it works against the brakes.
options.rationale: The student locates the temperature rise in the engine rather than at the friction between the brakes and the wheel.

options.text: The brakes cool so quickly that they seize onto the wheel.
options.rationale: The student recalls that braking changes the brakes' temperature but gets the direction of the change the wrong way round.

options.text: The brakes overheat and become less able to stop the lorry.
options.rationale: Each stop transfers energy to the thermal store of the brakes. Repeated large decelerations overheat them, which is one of the dangers the specification names.

options.text: The tyres heat up, which makes them grip the road better.
options.rationale: The student knows friction produces heating but treats the effect as helpful, and looks at the tyres rather than the brakes.

mcqs.stem: (Higher Tier) A car of mass 1000 kg slows from 20 m/s to rest in a distance of 25 m. Use v2 - u2 = 2 a s to estimate the average braking force on the car.

options.rationale: The student drops the factor of 2 from the equation, getting a deceleration of 16 m/s2 instead of 8 m/s2.
The student divides the speed by the distance, 20/25 = 0.8, and treats that as the acceleration.
The student works out the kinetic energy, 0.5 x 1000 x 400 = 200 000 J, and quotes that number in newtons.
0 - 400 = 2 x a x 25 gives a = -8 m/s2, and resultant force = mass x acceleration = 1000 x 8 = 8000 N.

mcqs.stem: (Higher Tier) A car of mass 1200 kg makes an emergency stop from 13 m/s, coming to rest in 4.0 s. Estimate the average braking force on the car.

options.rationale: Acceleration = change in velocity / time = 13 / 4.0 = 3.25 m/s2, so force = mass x acceleration = 1200 x 3.25 = 3900 N.
The student multiplies mass by velocity, which gives the momentum in kg m/s, not the force.
The student substitutes the time of 4.0 s into F = m a in place of the acceleration.
The student divides the mass by the time instead of multiplying the mass by the acceleration.
